From Wiktionary, the free dictionary
See also: Curry

English

[edit]

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • enPR: kŭrʹē
  • IPA(key): /ˈkʌ.ɹi/ (Received Pronunciation; US, without the hurry–furry merger)
    • Audio (US):(file)
  • (US, hurry–furry merger) IPA(key): /kɝ.i/
  • IPA(key): /ˈkʊ.ɹi/ (Northern England)
  • (Indic) IPA(key): /ˈkari/, (spelling pronunciation) /-ɾi/
  • Rhymes: -ʌɹi
  • Rhymes: -ʊəɹi

Etymology 1

[edit]

1747 (as currey, first published recipe for the dish in English[1][2]), from Tamil கறி (kaṟi), influenced by existing Middle English cury (“cooking”),[2] from Middle French cuyre (“to cook”) (whence also cuisine), from Vulgar Latin cocere, from Latin coquere.

Earlier cury found in 1390 cookbook Forme of Cury (Forms of Cooking) by court chefs of Richard II of England.

Alternative forms

[edit]
  • currey (obsolete)
  • currie (archaic)

Noun

[edit]

curry (countable and uncountable, plural curries)

  1. One of a family of dishes originating from Indian cuisine, flavored by a spiced sauce.
    Synonym: (rhyming slang) Ruby Murray
  2. A spiced sauce or relish, especially one flavored with curry powder.
  3. Curry powder.
    Synonym: curry powder
  4. (incel slang, derogatory, ethnic slur) A person of South Asian heritage.
    • 2020, Anthony Glyn Burton, "'I would do anything to not call this place home': The black pill, involuntary celibacy, and the neoliberal male grasp in digital incel communities", thesis submitted to Ryerson University & York University, pages 92-93:
      […] while another tells us that white women “are also THE most racist group of foids. they would rather put a bullet through their brain than date a curry or sandcel.”
    • 2020, Joshua A. Segalewitz, "'You Don’t Understand... It’s Not About Virginity': Sexual Markets, Identity Construction, and Violent Masculinity on an Incel Forum Board", thesis submitted to the University of Dayton, pages 29-30:
      For example, spicycurry says, “STOP THE COPE NOW. The only ones who should be complaining about race are us curries who are literally at the bottom of the pile.”
    • 2024, anonymous, quoted in Václav Báča, "Hierarchy at the Bottom of the Hierarchy: Involuntary Celibates, Identity, and Race", thesis submitted to Charles University, page 40:
      People get mixed up by thinking race is #1 because girls aren't going for asians and curries.
    • For more quotations using this term, see Citations:curry.

Verb

[edit]

curry (third-person singular simple present curries, present participle currying, simple past and past participle curried)

  1. (transitive) To cook or season with curry powder.
Translations
[edit]
to cook or season with curry
  • Esperanto: karei
  • Finnish: maustaa currylla

Etymology 2

[edit]

From Middle English currayen, from Old French correer (“to prepare”), presumably from Vulgar Latin *conredare, from Latin com- (a form of con- (“with; together”)) + a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *raidaz. More at ready.

Verb

[edit]

curry (third-person singular simple present curries, present participle currying, simple past and past participle curried)

  2. (transitive) To groom (a horse); to dress or rub down a horse with a curry comb.
    • 1610–1614, John Fletcher, “The Tragedie of Valentinian”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London: […] Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act II, scene i:
      Your short horse is soon curried.
    • 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter XI, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y.; London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
      One day I was out in the barn and he drifted in. I was currying the horse and he set down on the wheelbarrow and begun to ask questions.
  3. (transitive) To dress (leather) after it is tanned by beating, rubbing, scraping and colouring.
  4. (transitive) To beat, thrash; to drub.
    • c. 1619–1621, John Fletcher, “The Island Princesse”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London: […] Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, Act IV, scene ii:
      I have seen him curry a fellow's carcase handsomely.
    • 1662 (indicated as 1663), [Samuel Butler], “[The First Part of Hudibras]. Canto I.”, in Hudibras. The First and Second Parts. […], London: […] John Martyn and Henry Herringman, […], published 1678, →OCLC; republished in A[lfred] R[ayney] Waller, editor, Hudibras: Written in the Time of the Late Wars, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire: University Press, 1905, →OCLC:
      […] By setting brother against brother / To claw and curry one another.
  5. (transitive, figurative) To try to win or gain (favour) by flattering.
    • 2014 August 27, Stephanie Zacharek, “The Last of Robin Hood Wrestles with a Star's Underage Love”, in The Village Voice‎[2], archived from the original on 3 September 2014:
      A middle-aged woman waves and calls to her, as if she, like the hungry reporters, were currying the girl's favor: Florence Aadland (Sarandon, in a wily, multilayered performance), Beverly's mother, wears an expression of maternal concern, though her self-serving motives become increasingly clear.
Usage notes
[edit]
  • The sense to win or gain favor is most frequently used in the phrases to curry favor (with) and to curry [someone's] favor.

[edit]
  • curry favor

Etymology 3

[edit]

Named after American mathematician Haskell Curry.

Verb

[edit]

curry (third-person singular simple present curries, present participle currying, simple past and past participle curried)

  1. (transitive, computing) To perform currying upon.
    • 2011, Zachary Kessin, Programming HTML5 Applications: Building Powerful Cross-Platform Environments in JavaScript, "O'Reilly Media, Inc.", →ISBN, page 21:
      The easiest way to curry parameters is to create a function that takes a parameter block and returns a function that will call the original function with the presupplied parameters as defaults […] .
    • 2015, Leonardo Borges, Clojure Reactive Programming, Packt Publishing Ltd, →ISBN, page 194:
      Next, we curry the avg function to 3 arguments and put it into an option.
Derived terms
[edit]
  • uncurry
Translations
[edit]
to perform currying upon
  • Finnish: suorittaa Curry-muunnos
  • German: schönfinkeln, curryen
  • Polish: rozwijać funkcję impf, rozwinąć funkcję pf

Etymology 4

[edit]

Possibly derived from currier, a common 16th- to 18th-century form of courier, as if to ride post, to post. Possibly influenced by scurry.

Verb

[edit]

curry (third-person singular simple present curries, present participle currying, simple past and past participle curried)

  1. (intransitive, obsolete) To scurry; to ride or run hastily
  2. (transitive, obsolete) To cover (a distance); (of a projectile) to traverse (its range).
    • 1608, George Chapman, The Conspiracie, and Tragedie of Charles Duke of Byron, section 2.245:
      I am not hee that can ... by midnight leape my horse, curry seauen miles.
    • 1662, Thomas Salusbury, Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (Dialogue Two)
      All these shots shall curry or finish their ranges in times equal to each other.
  3. (transitive, obsolete) To hurry.
    • 1676, Andrew Marvell, Mr. Smirke, section 34:
      A sermon is soon curryed over.

French

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Borrowed into Middle French from multiple sources including English curry, all ultimately derived from Tamil கறி (kaṟi).

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ky.ʁi/
  • Audio:(file)
  • Audio (France (Lyon)):(file)

Noun

[edit]

curry m (plural currys)

  1. curry
    Synonym: cari

[edit]
